posts.cooked:
Playing every day, sitting in LFG trying to find partners, and never forming a consistent team makes climbing rating nearly impossible.

LFG is fine for getting random players into games, but once you start facing coordinated teams with established synergy, you hit a wall.

I’ve been on my Resto Druid at 1985 CR for two hours tonight and haven’t played a single game. I have over 100 people added on BattleTag, and they can all see my Quick Join listing — still nothing.

Gladiator in 3v3 needs to be more accessible.

When players put in effort, improve, and participate daily but still make no progress — especially in a mode that isn’t balanced because the game is primarily PvE‑focused — it creates a system where people gatekeep and sell Gladiator for real money to those willing to break TOS.

It shouldn’t be this hard to climb using the in‑game LFG tool.

Players like me, who can’t reach the goal without consistent partners, end up frustrated and ready to quit. The bracket becomes toxic because no one wants to queue with anyone even slightly lower CR, since MMR volatility punishes you for losing with lower‑rated players.

If Blizzard wants to retain players and keep the game healthy, Gladiator needs to be easier to reach

The whole “people want Gladiator for logging in” angle is just a strawman.

Nobody is asking for free rewards or participation trophies. What players are actually frustrated about is how much the current system depends on having consistent partners, meta comps, and a stable schedule — things that a lot of people simply don’t have access to.

You can play well, improve, and put in the time, and still watch your rating tank because you’re stuck in LFG roulette, especially as a healer.

The issue isn’t entitlement, it’s structure.

The ladder doesn’t reliably reward individual performance anymore. It rewards who you queue with, what comp you happen to land on, and whether your partners stick around for more than three games.

Pointing that out isn’t whining — it’s valid criticism of a system that punishes the people who actually try to climb without premades. Mocking that doesn’t fix anything; it just avoids the real conversation.

At some point, players stop asking “how do I get better” and start asking “why am I even doing this.” That’s not whining. That’s a completely reasonable reaction to a ladder that doesn’t reward the effort you put into it.

Darkjim:

I’ll bite. What is your actual recommendation, Velisen? What do you propose Blizzard do?

I don’t think the solution is “just queue more.” The problem isn’t effort — it’s that the current 3v3 system punishes anyone trying to climb as a solo healer through LFG. Every time I queue on any of my healers, I’m dealing with constant partner turnover, inconsistent synergy, and MMR swings that push me further away from my goal even when I’m playing well. Blizzard said rating gains were improved a few weeks ago, but in practice I’m still losing several CR per loss and barely gaining anything per win. That creates a loop where the more I try, the further I fall.

If Blizzard wants more people to participate in 3v3 and actually enjoy the climb, they need to address the structural disadvantage that solo healers face. The most realistic fix would be a role‑based MMR system for healers in LFG, where your rating isn’t dragged down by random DPS partners you’ll never see again. Healers deal with more responsibility and more variance, so their gains and losses should reflect that instead of being tied 1:1 to the performance of two strangers.

On top of that, Blizzard could adjust healer rating gains/losses to be more forgiving (+14 to +16 for wins, –8 to –10 for losses), add LFG protections when a DPS leaves early, and consider a slightly lower Gladiator threshold for solo healers compared to premade teams. None of this makes Gladiator “free” — it just makes the climb fair for the people who have the hardest path in the entire bracket.

Right now, the system creates a situation where players put in effort, lose rating anyway, and eventually lose the desire to queue at all. Blizzard needs to ask themselves why anyone would keep playing a mode where trying harder just means falling further behind. A healthier ladder isn’t about handing out rewards — it’s about making sure players don’t burn out and quit before they ever have a real chance.

posts.name: CardinalFang
posts.cooked:
Velisen:

I don’t think the solution is “just queue more.” The problem isn’t effort — it’s that the current 3v3 system punishes anyone trying to climb as a solo healer through LFG. Every time I queue on any of my healers, I’m dealing with constant partner turnover, inconsistent synergy, and MMR swings that push me further away from my goal even when I’m playing well. Blizzard said rating gains were improved a few weeks ago, but in practice I’m still losing several CR per loss and barely gaining anything per win. That creates a loop where the more I try, the further I fall.

Most of these issues are interpersonal problems rather than system design flaws. When Blizzard eliminated formal Arena Team rosters, they also eliminated the underlying “skin in the game” that those rosters created. I understand and agree with why they did, but now, it’s created a scenario where most players are seeking the “path of least resistance” to obtain their goals. Which translates into group hopping until they find a group they perceive will make their grind the easiest.

I do think Blizzard should add a 2v2 and 3v3 flex queue option. But the results will the same, it just will simplify the search.

Velisen:

If Blizzard wants more people to participate in 3v3 and actually enjoy the climb, they need to address the structural disadvantage that solo healers face. The most realistic fix would be a role‑based MMR system for healers in LFG, where your rating isn’t dragged down by random DPS partners you’ll never see again. Healers deal with more responsibility and more variance, so their gains and losses should reflect that instead of being tied 1:1 to the performance of two strangers.

Playing devil’s advocate, you could theoretically say the “structural” disadvantage also applies to DPS players. Healers typically hold all of the cards as the role population is smaller and more in demand. Therefore, healers have more opportunities presented to them than DPS players. Therefore, the argument could be made that all roles have advantages/disadvantages on how it pertains to Arena.

Velisen:

On top of that, Blizzard could adjust healer rating gains/losses to be more forgiving (+14 to +16 for wins, –8 to –10 for losses), add LFG protections when a DPS leaves early, and consider a slightly lower Gladiator threshold for solo healers compared to premade teams. None of this makes Gladiator “free” — it just makes the climb fair for the people who have the hardest path in the entire bracket.

This would cause Blizzard to manage so many nuances and variables in their MMR system and will create the situation where people basically “fail upwards”. This is what occured in Blitz this season. Players would get so much MMR per win that they would have such a massive cushion that they would achieve high ratings with losing records. That should not occur in my opinion.

Furthermore, incentivizing “solo” healing in LFG for organized 3s for rating/mmr benefits would create essentially an offshoot of RSS as healers would seek to just use LFG options provided to them for an easier grind rather than seeking to fraternize with partners, build synergy and grind together.

Velisen:

Right now, the system creates a situation where players put in effort, lose rating anyway, and eventually lose the desire to queue at all. Blizzard needs to ask themselves why anyone would keep playing a mode where trying harder just means falling further behind. A healthier ladder isn’t about handing out rewards — it’s about making sure players don’t burn out and quit before they ever have a real chance.

I don’t really have a response to this one way or the other. It’s a video game to me. I achieve a rating I want and call it a day. If I can’t achieve it, I try harder, and I fail, it is what it is. The bigger issue with modern PvP is that there is no incentive to queue for 80% of the season because of the nature of how MMR works. What they need to do is to shorten seasons and incentivize queueing every week for the entirety of the given season.

A PvP seasonal track and shorter seasons would keep players more engaged throughout the season and not cause bracket bottlenecks and player activity stagnation periods. Furthermore, it would psychosocially give players a more consistent feel of gratification in terms of progression rather than 3 dudes logging on in the last 2 weeks, max gearing and grinding gladiator.

You may not agree with my response, but I hope you respect it as I think cordial conversation is necessary for general imrovements.

posts.cooked:
I mean, yes — I do want Gladiator. That’s the whole point of playing the bracket. But wanting a reward doesn’t automatically make the argument invalid.

The issue isn’t “I want thing, therefore thing must be easier.” The issue is that the current system only works for players who already have stable partners, established synergy, and a premade environment. If you rely on LFG, you can put in the same effort, the same hours, and the same improvement — and still hit a wall because the system doesn’t support solo players.

Wanting Gladiator to be more accessible isn’t about entitlement. It’s about retention and fairness.

If players queue every day, improve, participate, and still make no progress because they can’t form consistent teams, eventually they stop queuing. And when people stop queuing, the bracket dies.

So yes, I want Gladiator — and I want a system where effort actually leads somewhere. That’s not bias. That’s a reasonable expectation for any competitive ladder that wants to stay alive.
